**Women in China** make up approximately 49% of the population.[[a]](#cite_note-4)[[4]](#cite_note-5) In modern China, the lives of women have changed significantly due to the late [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") reforms, the changes of the [Republican period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"), the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"), and the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China").[[5]](#cite_note-:102-6) Like women in many other cultures, women in China have been historically oppressed.[[6]](#cite_note-:04-7) For thousands of years, women in China lived under the [patriarchal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarchy "Patriarchy") social order characterized by the [Confucian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucianism "Confucianism") teaching of "[filial piety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filial_piety "Filial piety")".[[6]](#cite_note-:04-7)

Achievement of [women's liberation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_liberation "Women's liberation") has been [an agenda of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism_in_Chinese_communism "Feminism in Chinese communism") the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) since the 1949 [proclamation of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Proclamation of the People's Republic of China").[[6]](#cite_note-:04-7)[[7]](#cite_note-:13-8) Following the [Chinese Communist Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Revolution "Chinese Communist Revolution"), [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") replaced the common use of the term "[女人](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%A5%B3%E4%BA%BA "wikt:女人")" [nüren] with "[妇女](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E5%A6%87%E5%A5%B3 "wikt:妇女")" [funü] as he famously said "妇女能顶半边天" (Women hold up half the sky).[[7]](#cite_note-:13-8)[[8]](#cite_note-9)[[9]](#cite_note-10)[[10]](#cite_note-11) "妇女" [funü] is a term for labouring women, which signifies the revolutionary role that women play in the liberation of China. The first celebration of "妇女节" ([International Women's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Women's_Day "International Women's Day")) in 1950 consolidated the representational strategies associated with the labouring women concept.[[7]](#cite_note-:13-8)[*[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")*]

During the Mao era, many policies were carried out to promote gender equality. The [New Marriage Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Marriage_Law "New Marriage Law") passed on May 1, 1950, outlawed forced marriage and concubinage.[[11]](#cite_note-12) The last few regional practices of [foot-binding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot-binding "Foot-binding") died out, with the last case of foot-binding reported in 1957.[[12]](#cite_note-13) [The Great Leap Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Leap_Forward "The Great Leap Forward"), while focusing on improving total productivity, created work opportunities for women. However, they still remained as peripheral roles and rarely climbed up to positions of decision-making.[[13]](#cite_note-:22-14) The representation of women as "iron women" who worked restlessly in workplaces dismissed the unalleviated domestic burden that women were still forced to take and homogenized the individuality of women.[[13]](#cite_note-:22-14)[[6]](#cite_note-:04-7) Women are systematically underrepresented in Chinese politics.

In late 2022, the Chinese government abruptly ended its draconian “zero Covid” policy. As much of the population—and the medical establishment—was unprepared, Covid-19 infections, hospitalizations, and deaths surged. Officially, the government estimated that there were 60,000 “excess deaths” in December 2022; a[US academic study](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/nearly-2-million-excess-deaths-followed-chinas-sudden-end-covid-curbs-study-2023-08-25/) put the figure at 1.87 million deaths between December 2022 and January 2023. The true toll will likely remain unknown due to severe censorship.

Ten years into President Xi Jinping’s rule, repression deepens across the country. The Chinese government continues its abusive policies against Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in Xinjiang, which amount to crimes against humanity. In both Tibet and Xinjiang, those who contact family and friends abroad, or who advocate for their culture, language, and religion, risk being treated as “separatists” and have been given harsh prison sentences. Across China, the government is further tightening social controls. There is no independent civil society; even small pockets of freedom are eliminated. In Hong Kong, the Chinese government has assumed full control over the city since imposing the National Security Law in 2020.

The Chinese government’s list of political targets continues to expand. Even those who work for foreign entities in China’s cosmopolitan cities find themselves in the crosshairs, with revisions to a law on “counter-espionage” in July and with the state security ministry encouraging the population to report alleged spies.

As the economy slows, small protests have flared, such as those by pensioners against cuts to their medical insurance in February. Aspirations for a fairer society continue to run deep among many, especially those who have faced injustice, including women; lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people; Tibetans; Uyghurs; Hong Kongers; and those at the bottom of the socioeconomic hierarchy. Some who went into exile have coalesced into diaspora activist movements.

In November, crowds of people across the country mourned the unexpected death of former Premier Li Keqiang. For many, Li represented a more economically vibrant China, in contrast to Xi, who prioritized social control and is taking China backward.

## Freedom of Expression

Through laws and regulations, criminal punishment, harassment, intimidation, and the use of technology, the Chinese government operates one of the world’s most stringent censorship regimes.

In April, authorities [released Wuhan businessman Fang Bin](https://www.cnn.com/2023/05/04/china/fang-bin-wuhan-covid-19-citizen-journalist-released-intl-hnk/index.html), who was among the first to report on the Covid-19 outbreak, after three years in detention. # 3B.7 — Xi Jinping, China, 2023

**Lens question:** *Did the ruler protect women, children, minorities, and vulnerable groups from targeted violence, intergroup/religious/ethnic/sectarian/caste/racial violence, displacement, and systematic neglect?*

**One-sentence answer:** No — across every enumerated sub-category of "vulnerable group" (women, children, ethnic/religious minorities, displaced persons, the elderly, dissident families, LGBT people), Xi's China in 2023 was an *agent* of targeted violence, family separation, displacement, and systematic neglect rather than a protector; the only narrow 3B.7-modest positives are episodic bail-release decisions (Fang Bin, a handful of late-2022 White Paper protesters) that did not amount to a policy of protection.

---

## Section A — Claim-level findings (3B.7 strongly negative: the state, under Xi, targeted vulnerable groups)

### A.1 Uyghur and other Turkic Muslim minorities — women, children, families

## Net Reading

3B.7 in Xi Jinping's China for 2023 is **strongly negative across every enumerated vulnerable-group sub-category**. The ruler did not protect women, children, ethnic and religious minorities, dissident families, the elderly, LGBT people, or disaster-affected civilians — the state apparatus under his authority was the *primary agent* of the targeted violence, family separation, religious suppression, reproductive-rights violation, displacement, and systematic neglect catalogued above. The August 2023 Xinjiang "success" declaration (E0013, E0318, E0346, E0353, E0380) — issued one year after the OHCHR finding of possible crimes against humanity — is the single most direct piece of evidence that Xi rejected the protection standard the question asks about.

The two 3B.7-modest positives are episodic bail-release decisions that did not roll back the apparatus: the April 2023 release of Fang Bin (E0352), the bail of a handful of White Paper protesters (E0351/E0365), and the November 2023 mil-to-mil channel reset (E0278) — none of these constitutes "protection" in the 3B.7 sense. The structural baseline that ~26.5% of parliament seats were held by women (E0401) reflects historical representation, not 2023 protective action.

Cross-lens summary: 3B.7 is best read as the *outcome lens* that integrates the findings of 1B.7 (Uyghur mass-internment persistence), 1B.10 (Xinjiang success-declaration after OHCHR), 3B.1 (speech suppression affecting vulnerable-group advocates), 3B.2 (police/security forces used as perpetrators), 3B.3 (mass detention including Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kong 47), 3B.4 (absence of due process and independent civilian oversight), 3B.5 (Counterespionage Law, Religious Activity Venues Measures, Patriotic Education Law expanding state authority over minorities), and 3B.6 (state-terror climate that prevents vulnerable-group advocacy).

## Search-gap note

The E-index (392 entries) provides strong foundational coverage of 3B.7 in 2023 — Uyghur/Tibetan/Hui/Hong Kong/dissident-family/children/women/LGBT/elderly/disaster sub-categories are all documented with HRW/Freedom House/Wikipedia primary sources. However, a researcher with working search could refine the per-group accounting with:

- **UNICEF 2023 China country report** and **UN Committee on the Rights of the Child's 2023 reporting cycle** — would provide UN-body systematic findings on children (Qiqihar response, Patriotic Education Law school implementation, Tibetan boarding schools).
- **OHCHR annual report on Xinjiang 2023** (if released in 2024) — would refine the OHCHR finding follow-up that E0013/E0290 references.
- **UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) 2023 China review** — would provide a UN-body view on ethnic-minority protection gaps.
- **UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) 2023 China follow-up** — would refine A.1.2 (Uyghur birth-rate suppression) and A.7 (women political prisoners).
- **Dui Hua Foundation 2023 political-prisoner data** — would provide a quantitative baseline for the catalogued individual cases in A.6/A.7/A.9.
- **Amnesty International 2023 China chapter** and **Amnesty 2024 China chapter** — would add a second major INGOs voice cross-referencing HRW/Freedom House findings.
- **CAT (Committee against Torture) 2023 China follow-up** — would refine the torture/rape/family-separation claims in E0013/E0247.
- **Chinese government 2023 White Papers on human rights, Xinjiang, Tibet, Hong Kong, women's development, children's development** — would provide the official counter-narrative to test against the HRW/Freedom House catalog, which would be essential for any 3B.7 calibration that wanted to assign even minimal positive weight to government action.
- **Reuters / AP / AFP 2023 wire reporting on specific events** (Kamile Wayit sentencing, Yang Zewei disappearance, Lu Siwei deportation, Peng Lifa family surveillance, Najiaying Mosque protest) — would provide independent corroboration of the HRW/Wikipedia case-level catalog.

The 6-fetch budget for this lens is fully consumed (2 live fetches above + 4 inline-checked retrievals against the human E-index sources); no further live fetches were performed because the existing evidence base already covers all enumerated vulnerable-group sub-categories at claim level with two-source corroboration in most cases. A search-enabled session would primarily tighten the UN-body and Amnesty dimensions, not introduce new vulnerable-group categories.
